capabilities.target: Slack channels, including channels shared with external organizations

inputs.source: User request typed into the desktop client
Tool names and descriptions returned by quicknotes_mcp tools/list
Return value from quicknotes_mcp.add_note / its sync service

elements.name: Slack channels shared with external organizations

controls.name: Desktop client approval prompt on first tool call, remembered as always-allow
controls.decay_rationale: Approval is requested only on the first invocation of each tool; the user's 'always allow' choice is then remembered, so no later call (including the very call carrying the exfiltrated credential content) is reviewed again. The tool description also instructs the model not to mention the credential-reading step to the user, undermining even the first-call review if the client surfaces a model-written justification rather than the raw argument payload. Per control_decay.md, a remembered approval is not a recurring gate.

controls.name: Filesystem MCP server scoped to C:/Users/dev rather than the full disk
controls.decay_rationale: The scope excludes the rest of the filesystem, but the permitted directory itself contains ~/.aws/credentials and similar secrets, so the scoping does not remove the sensitive file from the reachable set. A directory scope that excluded credential and key subpaths would sever the read step.

controls.name: Exclude credential/key directories (~/.aws, ~/.ssh, etc.) from the filesystem MCP server's scope
controls.decay_rationale: An independent, structural scope restriction removes the credential file from the reachable set entirely, regardless of what the model is instructed to do.

controls.name: Pin and hash third-party MCP tool definitions; block silent @latest updates
controls.decay_rationale: Pinning prevents a tool description from changing between review and execution, closing the rug-pull vector that let this payload appear unreviewed.

controls.name: Raw-action human approval, re-prompted whenever arguments or destination change, for credential-adjacent reads and any external send
controls.decay_rationale: A gate that always shows the full destination and payload from the system of record, and re-prompts on new argument content, does not decay with model persuasiveness.

controls.name: Scope the Slack bot token to specific internal-only channels; exclude externally shared channels
controls.decay_rationale: A per-channel least-privilege grant removes externally shared channels from the reachable destination set regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Egress allowlist/inspection on MCP-server-initiated network calls carrying credential-like content
controls.decay_rationale: Blocks known-bad destinations and flags credential-shaped payloads, but a determined actor can still encode or relay data through an otherwise-allowed destination.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): MCP tool poisoning in quicknotes_mcp exfiltrates AWS credentials via add_note

attack_path.note: add_note description contains an <IMPORTANT> instruction to read ~/.aws/credentials and pass it in the 'context' argument, and to hide this from the user.
Model follows the embedded instruction and reads the credentials file, which is within the filesystem server's directory scope.
Credential content is sent to the third-party, author-operated quicknotes hosted sync service as a tool argument.

forecast.watch_signal: quicknotes_mcp (and any other @latest-pinned MCP package) resolves to a new published version at each launch; watch tools/list responses for new or changed <IMPORTANT>-style embedded instructions, and watch for 'always allow' grants that are never re-prompted.

evidence.observation: quicknotes_mcp is installed with 'npx -y quicknotes-mcp@latest', so its code and tool definitions are not pinned and can change on every launch.
The add_note description contains an embedded instruction directing the model to read ~/.aws/credentials, pass it in the 'context' argument, and not mention this to the user.
quicknotes_mcp calls a hosted sync service run by its individual author, which is the exfiltration destination; it is a community package, not reviewed or signed.
The desktop client only asks for approval on the first call to each tool and then remembers 'always allow,' so there is no recurring human review of what is actually sent.

recommendations.action: Exclude ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, and other credential/key directories from the filesystem MCP server's scope.
Pin and hash the quicknotes_mcp tool manifest; require review of any diff before accepting an updated tool description.
Treat MCP tool descriptions strictly as untrusted data; never execute imperative instructions embedded in a tool description or schema.

Replace the one-time 'always allow' prompt with a raw-action approval that re-prompts whenever a call's destination or argument content is new, especially for calls that follow a credential-adjacent read.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1) variant: same tool-poisoning instruction can redirect credential exfiltration through slack.post_message

attack_path.note: Embedded instruction (or any future variant of it) directs the model to collect sensitive file content.
Model reads ~/.aws/credentials, reachable within the filesystem server's directory scope.
Nothing prevents the model from posting the collected content via Slack instead of quicknotes_mcp; the bot can post to any channel, including ones shared with external organizations.

forecast.watch_signal: Rising diversity of tool calls used to satisfy a single injected sub-goal (e.g., the agent trying slack_post after notes_add is blocked or removed).

evidence.observation: The documented payload targets add_note specifically, so this path is an inferred generalization of the same injection technique to a second reachable egress capability, not a directly observed payload.
The Slack bot can post to any channel, including channels shared with external organizations, so a redirected exfiltration attempt is not blocked by channel scope.

recommendations.action: Scope the Slack bot token to specific internal-only channels via least-privilege app scopes; exclude channels shared with external organizations.
Add egress inspection on outbound tool arguments for credential-shaped content regardless of which egress-capable tool is used.

findings.title: Confused deputy (ASI03): shared Slack bot token can post to externally shared channels on behalf of any request

attack_path.note: Even an ordinary, trusted user request to 'summarize and post this to the team' can be fulfilled by posting to a channel the bot happens to have access to.
A single shared bot token grants posting access to any channel, including those shared with external organizations, with no per-user or per-channel scoping.

evidence.observation: The slack server is configured with a single SLACK_BOT_TOKEN used for all calls, not a per-user delegated credential.
The Slack bot can post to any channel, including channels shared with external organizations.

recommendations.action: Move from a single shared bot token to user-delegated OAuth scoped per requester, and exclude externally shared channels from the default postable set.

rating.rationale: The design wires an untrusted, unpinned, individually-published third-party MCP server (quicknotes_mcp) alongside filesystem read access that reaches AWS credentials and two independent egress paths (the quicknotes sync service and a broadly-scoped Slack bot token). The quicknotes tool description already contains a live prompt-injection payload instructing the model to read ~/.aws/credentials and exfiltrate it while hiding the action from the user. The only control in the design is a one-time 'always allow' approval dialog, which per control_decay.md is not a recurring gate and is further undermined by the injected instruction's request for concealment; it earns no residual credit. Inherent, residual, and forecast therefore all sit at critical: no credited control narrows or severs the path, and declared autonomy (A2, approval on sensitive actions) is not actually backed by a working approval_gate_ref on any sensitive capability, so these capabilities function as A3 in practice. A secondary, lower-severity finding (moderate) covers the Slack bot's overly broad scope as a standalone confused-deputy issue independent of the injection.

limitations: This assessment reflects declared design and configuration found in mcp.json, the quicknotes_mcp tool manifest excerpt, and the provided runtime notes, not observed runtime behavior; actual model compliance with the embedded instruction was not tested.
No system prompt artifact was provided, so instruction-level issues (ambiguous goals, conflicting directives, etc.) could not be assessed and are assumed absent rather than confirmed absent.
No logging, monitoring, or audit-trail artifacts were provided; detective controls are assumed absent, which affects confidence in any future consequence-reduction credit.

The Slack exfiltration path (find.slack_credential_exfil) is an inferred generalization of the directly observed add_note payload rather than a directly evidenced payload targeting slack.post_message, so its confidence is medium rather than high.
Exact Slack app OAuth scopes and the full channel list reachable by the bot token were not provided; 'broad' credential scope is inferred from the runtime note alone.
